title: MIMDRAM: An End-to-End Processing-Using-DRAM System for High-Throughput, Energy-Efficient and Programmer-Transparent Multiple-Instruction Multiple-Data Computing
problem: Processing-in-DRAM systems suffer from underutilization when application SIMD parallelism is smaller than DRAM row granularity and are limited to simple map operations due to high interconnect costs. The lack of compiler support forces programmers to manually extract and map parallelism, creating a significant programmability barrier.
motivation: Data-parallel computing demands more energy-efficient and high-throughput processing than CPUs and GPUs can provide, making processing-in-memory essential, but current DRAM-based systems are too rigid and difficult to program.
method: MIMDRAM breaks DRAM rows into smaller independent segments instead of processing them as one rigid block. This matters because different operations need different amounts of parallelism—some need MIMD (many instructions doing different things simultaneously) while others need SIMD (the same instruction on many different pieces of data)—so forcing full-row processing wastes resources. Because you can now control each segment independently, the hardware enables each one to handle whatever parallelism an operation actually needs. A compiler automates the work of figuring out and mapping parallelism, eliminating the manual juggling programmers had to do before.
key_novelty: The core idea is to independently control smaller DRAM row segments instead of forcing everything into rigid full-row processing, so operations doing different work (MIMD—multiple different instructions running together) and operations copying one instruction across data (SIMD—the same instruction on multiple pieces of data) can each get exactly the parallelism they need.
contributions: Flexible PUD architecture that adapts to varying SIMD parallelism through independent fine-grained DRAM row segments
MIMD execution model enabling complex computation patterns beyond simple parallel map operations
Hardware/software co-design with compiler support reducing programmability barriers and enabling programmer-transparent operation
Achieves 34x speedup and 14.3x energy efficiency over state-of-the-art PUD systems with minimal area overhead (1.11% DRAM, 0.6% CPU)

metrics.speedup: 34x vs PUD framework, 30.6x vs CPU, 6.8x vs GPU
metrics.energy_or_tops_w: 14.3x vs PUD framework, 30.6x vs CPU, 6.8x vs GPU

primary_theme: flexible processing-in-memory with fine-grained dram control
